ISLAMABAD, Pakistan (CNN)  -- Pakistan launched an offensive against the Taliban on Saturday, the biggest military push against militants in Pakistan's northwestern tribal region since a civilian government took power in March. A Pakistan army vehicle patrols a troubled district of South Waziristan, in the northwest of Pakistan. Army spokesman Gen. Athar Abbas said the operation occurred in the Khyber section of the tribal region, west of Peshawar, the capital of the North-West Frontier Province. And it comes as the new administration announced that it would get tough with radicals in the region. There had been reports that Peshawar was being threatened by militants. Although Abbas said the reports were exaggerated, the military determined that the conditions in the area necessitated action. Troops cleared three militant outposts and pushed the insurgents west, Abbas said. There were no immediate reports of militant resistance or any casualties. The area is not far from the Afghan-Pakistan border. The Taliban militant movement has a strong presence in the tribal region and in neighboring Afghanistan, and there also have been numerous attacks on that restive border in recent weeks. U.S. Secretary of Defense Robert Gates said this week that he hopes a newly announced Pakistani effort to clamp down on Islamic militants in its northwestern tribal districts will improve the situation in Afghanistan. "What has happened is that as various agreements have been negotiated or were in the process of negotiation with various groups by the Pakistani government ... the pressure was taken off of these people and these groups, and they've therefore been more free to be able to cross the border and create problems for us," he said at the Pentagon. Meanwhile, the the U.S.-led coalition in Afghanistan reported that 32 militants had been killed two days ago during Afghan and coalition operations in southern Afghanistan. The fighting occurred in Uruzgan province and the report comes amid Pentagon warnings of a "resilient insurgency" by the Taliban. Afghan and coalition forces were ambushed Thursday during a patrol. They returned fire and called in airstrikes that killed three militants. Soon after, the militants again attacked the patrol. The forces then killed 29 insurgents. "During this engagement, insurgents attempted to disguise themselves in women's clothing in order to escape," the coalition said. A child and two police officers were wounded. This is the latest report of fighting across Afghanistan, where there has been an uptick in Taliban militant activities in the south, the east, and the Afghan-Pakistan border region. On Friday, a coalition service member was killed in Farah province. The death toll of U.S. and allied troops killed in Afghanistan in June has reached 40, the highest monthly toll of the war. Also, NATO's International Security Assistance Force were attacked in Paktika and Kunar provinces. Strikes in Kunar killed two civilians and wounded 11 others. Insurgents in both Pakistan and Afghanistan fired rockets at the Paktika base, but there were no casualties reported. A Pentagon report on security in Afghanistan underscored the tenacity of the Taliban. It said that although there has been some progress in battling the Taliban, setbacks are expected. Although NATO and Afghan force operations kept the insurgency down in 2007 by killing or capturing key leaders and clearing out Taliban safe havens, the report predicted that the Taliban would be back in 2008.

outputs.L1:
ISLAMABAD, Pakistan (CNN) — Pakistan launched an offensive against the Taliban on Saturday, marking the largest military push against militants in the country’s northwestern tribal region since a civilian government took power in March.

A Pakistani army vehicle patrolled a troubled district of South Waziristan, in northwestern Pakistan. Army spokesman Gen. Athar Abbas said the operation took place in the Khyber section of the tribal region, west of Peshawar, the capital of the North-West Frontier Province.

The offensive comes as the new administration announced that it would take a tougher stance against radicals in the region. There had been reports that militants were threatening Peshawar. Although Abbas said those reports were exaggerated, the military determined that conditions in the area required action.

Troops cleared three militant outposts and pushed the insurgents west, Abbas said. There were no immediate reports of militant resistance or casualties. The area is not far from the Afghan-Pakistan border.

The Taliban militant movement has a strong presence in the tribal region and in neighboring Afghanistan, and there have been numerous attacks along that volatile border in recent weeks.

U.S. Secretary of Defense Robert Gates said this week that he hoped a newly announced Pakistani effort to clamp down on Islamic militants in its northwestern tribal districts would improve the situation in Afghanistan.

“What has happened is that as various agreements have been negotiated or were in the process of negotiation with various groups by the Pakistani government ... the pressure was taken off of these people and these groups, and they’ve therefore been more free to be able to cross the border and create problems for us,” he said at the Pentagon.

Meanwhile, the U.S.-led coalition in Afghanistan reported that 32 militants had been killed two days earlier during Afghan and coalition operations in southern Afghanistan. The fighting occurred in Uruzgan province, and the report came amid Pentagon warnings of a “resilient insurgency” by the Taliban.

Afghan and coalition forces were ambushed Thursday during a patrol. They returned fire and called in airstrikes, which killed three militants. Soon afterward, the militants attacked the patrol again. The forces then killed 29 insurgents.

“During this engagement, insurgents attempted to disguise themselves in women’s clothing in order to escape,” the coalition said.

A child and two police officers were wounded.

This is the latest report of fighting across Afghanistan, where Taliban militant activity has increased in the south, the east, and the Afghan-Pakistan border region.

On Friday, a coalition service member was killed in Farah province. The death toll among U.S. and allied troops killed in Afghanistan in June has reached 40, the highest monthly toll of the war.

NATO’s International Security Assistance Force was also attacked in Paktika and Kunar provinces. Strikes in Kunar killed two civilians and wounded 11 others. Insurgents in both Pakistan and Afghanistan fired rockets at the Paktika base, but no casualties were reported.

A Pentagon report on security in Afghanistan underscored the Taliban’s tenacity. It said that although some progress had been made in battling the Taliban, setbacks were expected. While NATO and Afghan force operations kept the insurgency in check in 2007 by killing or capturing key leaders and clearing Taliban safe havens, the report predicted that the Taliban would return in 2008.
outputs.L2:
ISLAMABAD, Pakistan (CNN) — On Saturday, Pakistan began a military campaign against the Taliban, marking the largest operation targeting militants in the country’s northwestern tribal areas since a civilian administration assumed power in March.

A Pakistani army vehicle was seen patrolling a tense area of South Waziristan in Pakistan’s northwest. Military spokesman Gen. Athar Abbas said the operation took place in the Khyber area of the tribal belt, located west of Peshawar, the capital of North-West Frontier Province.

The action followed an announcement by Pakistan’s new government that it intended to take a firmer stance against extremists in the region. Reports had suggested that militants were posing a threat to Peshawar. Abbas said those accounts had been overstated, but added that the army concluded the situation on the ground required intervention.

According to Abbas, Pakistani troops dismantled three militant positions and forced the fighters to retreat westward. There were no immediate accounts of resistance from militants or reports of casualties.

The area lies relatively close to the border between Pakistan and Afghanistan. Taliban fighters have a significant presence both in Pakistan’s tribal areas and across the border in Afghanistan, and the unsettled frontier has seen many attacks in recent weeks.

Earlier in the week, U.S. Defense Secretary Robert Gates said he hoped Pakistan’s newly announced plan to crack down on Islamic militants in its northwestern tribal districts would help improve conditions in Afghanistan.

“What has happened is that as various agreements have been negotiated or were in the process of negotiation with various groups by the Pakistani government ... the pressure was taken off of these people and these groups, and they've therefore been more free to be able to cross the border and create problems for us,” Gates said at the Pentagon.

At the same time, the U.S.-led coalition in Afghanistan said 32 militants had been killed two days earlier during operations conducted by Afghan and coalition forces in southern Afghanistan. The clashes took place in Uruzgan province, and the announcement came as the Pentagon warned of a “resilient insurgency” by the Taliban.

Afghan and coalition troops were ambushed Thursday while on patrol. They responded with gunfire and requested air support, which killed three militants. A short time later, militants launched another attack on the patrol, after which Afghan and coalition forces killed 29 more insurgents.

“During this engagement, insurgents attempted to disguise themselves in women's clothing in order to escape,” the coalition said.

A child and two police officers were injured.

The incident was the latest in a series of clashes across Afghanistan, where Taliban activity has increased in the south, the east, and along the Afghan-Pakistani border.

On Friday, a coalition service member died in Farah province. With that death, the number of U.S. and allied troops killed in Afghanistan during June rose to 40, making it the deadliest month of the war up to that point.

NATO’s International Security Assistance Force also came under attack in Paktika and Kunar provinces. Strikes in Kunar killed two civilians and injured 11 others. In Paktika, insurgents from both Pakistan and Afghanistan fired rockets at a base, though no casualties were reported.

A Pentagon assessment of security in Afghanistan emphasized the Taliban’s continued strength. The report said that while some gains had been made against the Taliban, further reversals were likely. It noted that NATO and Afghan military operations had limited the insurgency in 2007 by killing or capturing important leaders and eliminating Taliban sanctuaries, but it also forecast that the Taliban would reemerge in 2008.

The offensive comes amid growing concern over the strength of Taliban-linked militants operating near the Afghan-Pakistan border. Pakistan has launched its largest military offensive against Taliban militants in the northwestern Khyber tribal region since the country’s civilian government came to power, sending troops into the area to clear militant positions and reassert government control.

The operation targeted militant outposts in Khyber, a strategically important tribal district close to the city of Peshawar and near routes linking Pakistan with Afghanistan. Officials have long viewed the region as a key base for armed groups involved in attacks inside Pakistan, as well as in cross-border violence affecting Afghanistan.

According to the army, Pakistani forces cleared three militant outposts during the operation. There were no immediate reports of resistance from the militants, and no casualties were initially reported among security forces, civilians, or insurgents.

The offensive comes amid growing concern over militant activity near Peshawar, one of Pakistan’s most important northwestern cities, and over instability along the Afghan border. Taliban fighters and allied groups have used parts of the tribal belt as safe havens, taking advantage of the rugged terrain and limited state authority in the area.

The move is being seen as a significant step by the government and military to increase pressure on militants operating in Pakistan’s tribal regions. Those groups have been blamed for contributing to violence on both sides of the border, complicating security efforts for Pakistan and Afghanistan alike.

While the initial phase of the operation appeared to face little resistance, the broader challenge for Pakistani authorities remains maintaining control of cleared areas and preventing militants from regrouping. Past operations in the tribal regions have often displaced fighters temporarily, only for them to return once military pressure eased.

The Khyber offensive also underscores the difficult balance facing Pakistan’s civilian leadership and armed forces: responding to domestic security threats while managing the wider regional impact of militant networks that operate across the Pakistan-Afghanistan frontier.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news article about Pakistan launching a major offensive against Taliban militants in the Khyber tribal region, including details from the army spokesman, U.S. reactions, and related fighting in Afghanistan.
counterfactuals.output:
**Pakistan launches major offensive against Taliban militants in Khyber tribal region**

**Islamabad, Pakistan** — Pakistan’s military has launched a major ground and air offensive against Taliban-linked militants in the Khyber tribal region, a strategically important area along the Afghan border that has long served as a haven and transit route for insurgent groups, army officials said.

The operation, centered in parts of Khyber Agency including militant strongholds near the Tirah Valley and Bara area, is aimed at dismantling networks affiliated with the Pakistani Taliban and other extremist factions, according to the military.

Army spokesman Maj. Gen. Asim Bajwa said security forces were targeting militant hideouts, weapons depots and command centers, adding that the operation was part of a broader campaign to eliminate “terrorist sanctuaries” in Pakistan’s tribal belt.

“Troops are advancing in the area, and militants are being pursued wherever they are found,” Bajwa said in a statement. He said airstrikes and artillery were being used to soften militant positions before ground forces moved in.

The military said a number of militants had been killed in the opening phase of the operation, though independent confirmation was not immediately possible because journalists have limited access to the conflict zone. Officials also said civilians had been warned to leave areas where fighting was expected, raising concerns about a new wave of displacement from the already volatile tribal region.

Khyber has long been viewed as a critical corridor for militants moving between Pakistan and Afghanistan. It also lies near the route used to transport NATO supplies into Afghanistan, making control of the area a priority for both Pakistani authorities and Western officials.

In Washington, U.S. officials welcomed Pakistan’s action but emphasized the need for sustained pressure on militant groups operating on both sides of the border.

A U.S. State Department official said the United States supported Pakistan’s efforts to combat extremism and urged continued coordination with Afghan authorities to prevent militants from escaping across the frontier. U.S. officials have repeatedly pressed Pakistan to target all militant factions without distinction, including groups accused of launching attacks inside Afghanistan.

The offensive comes as Pakistani forces continue operations in other parts of the tribal belt, including North Waziristan, where the army began a large-scale campaign after years of pressure from Washington and a series of deadly attacks inside Pakistan.

Meanwhile, across the border in Afghanistan, Afghan security forces have been engaged in heavy fighting with Taliban insurgents in several eastern and southern provinces. Afghan officials have said militants fleeing Pakistani operations have attempted to cross into Afghanistan, while Afghan Taliban fighters have continued assaults on police posts, army bases and district centers.

The violence underscores the challenge facing both countries as insurgent groups exploit the porous border and rugged terrain to regroup and launch attacks.

Pakistan’s government says the latest offensive is part of a wider effort to reassert state control over the tribal regions, which for years operated under a separate legal system and where militant groups established parallel authority in some areas.

But analysts warn that clearing territory is only the first step. Holding it, preventing militants from returning and restoring civilian governance will be crucial to the long-term success of the campaign.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a full-length news report dated from Islamabad on Pakistan's new civilian government taking military action against militants near Peshawar, with background on Taliban activity along the Afghan-Pakistan border.
counterfactuals.output:
**ISLAMABAD, Pakistan —** Pakistan’s new civilian government has ordered a security operation against suspected militants in the country’s northwest, officials said, in one of the first major tests of its authority over a region long affected by Taliban violence and cross-border militancy from Afghanistan.

Security officials said the action was focused on militant hideouts in areas near **Peshawar**, the capital of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, close to the former tribal belt that borders Afghanistan. The operation reportedly involved paramilitary forces and police, backed by army units, after intelligence indicated that militants were regrouping and planning attacks on security personnel and government installations.

Government officials in Islamabad said the move was aimed at “restoring the writ of the state” and protecting civilians from armed groups operating in and around the provincial capital. They did not immediately provide details on casualties or arrests, and access to the affected areas remained limited.

The operation comes at a politically sensitive moment for Pakistan’s new civilian leadership, which is under pressure to respond to a rise in militant attacks while also managing economic strain, public frustration and a complicated relationship with the powerful military establishment. Pakistani governments have often struggled to balance negotiations, policing and military force in dealing with insurgent groups in the northwest.

Militant violence has increased in Pakistan since the Afghan Taliban returned to power in Kabul in 2021. Pakistani officials have repeatedly accused militants affiliated with the **Tehrik-i-Taliban Pakistan**, or TTP, of using sanctuaries across the Afghan border to plan attacks inside Pakistan. The Afghan Taliban government denies allowing its territory to be used against Pakistan, but tensions between Islamabad and Kabul have deepened over the issue.

The TTP, sometimes called the Pakistani Taliban, is a separate organization from the Afghan Taliban but shares ideological roots and long-standing ties with militant networks that operated on both sides of the frontier. The group has waged an insurgency against the Pakistani state for more than a decade, targeting soldiers, police, politicians, schools and civilians.

The region around Peshawar has been a frequent target of militant attacks. The city, a gateway to the Khyber Pass and Afghanistan beyond it, has endured years of bombings and raids. Nearby districts and former tribal areas were once strongholds for Pakistani Taliban factions, foreign fighters and sectarian militant groups before major military operations pushed many militants into remote mountain areas or across the border.

Analysts say the latest security operation reflects growing concern that militant networks are attempting to re-establish influence in parts of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. Police in the province have been frequent targets, with attacks on checkpoints, patrols and police stations rising in recent months.

The civilian government’s decision to authorize force is likely to draw both support and scrutiny. Many Pakistanis demand tougher action after repeated militant attacks, but past military campaigns in the northwest displaced large numbers of civilians and left communities wary of prolonged security operations.

Officials said the government would pair security action with efforts to strengthen local administration and policing. However, residents and rights groups have often complained that counterterrorism measures in the region lack transparency and can place civilians at risk.

The border with Afghanistan remains central to Pakistan’s security challenge. The rugged frontier, much of it mountainous and historically porous, has long allowed militants, smugglers and tribal networks to move between the two countries. Pakistan has fenced much of the border in recent years, but officials say infiltration and militant movement remain difficult to prevent.

Islamabad has urged Kabul to act against TTP leaders allegedly based in Afghanistan. Afghan Taliban officials have instead called for dialogue and deny that organized attacks are being launched from Afghan soil. The dispute has led to border closures, diplomatic protests and occasional armed clashes between Pakistani and Afghan forces.

For Pakistan’s new civilian administration, the operation near Peshawar may signal a harder line against militants. But security experts warn that military action alone is unlikely to end the insurgency without better intelligence, improved governance and a durable policy toward Afghanistan.

As the operation continued, authorities said security had been tightened in Peshawar and surrounding districts, with checkpoints reinforced and searches underway in suspected militant areas. The government said more details would be released after the completion of the action.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.output:
**Pakistani forces launch operation in northwest as coalition troops clash with Taliban in Afghanistan**

**ISLAMABAD, Pakistan (CNN-style wire report)** — Pakistani security forces have launched a new operation in the country’s northwest tribal belt, targeting suspected militant hideouts near the Afghan border, officials said, as coalition troops in neighboring Afghanistan reported fresh clashes with Taliban insurgents.

Pakistani military officials said the operation was focused on remote areas long used by militant groups to move fighters, weapons and supplies across the rugged frontier. Troops, backed by artillery and helicopter support, were deployed to search compounds and mountain routes believed to be linked to insurgent networks operating on both sides of the border.

There was no immediate independent confirmation of casualty figures. Access to Pakistan’s former tribal districts remains restricted, and journalists are often unable to verify battlefield claims.

Local residents reported intermittent shelling and said some families had begun leaving villages near the area of fighting. Pakistani authorities said security forces were attempting to avoid civilian casualties and had set up checkpoints to prevent militants from escaping.

The operation comes amid renewed concern over militant activity along the Pakistan-Afghanistan border, a region that has been a flashpoint for years. Islamabad has repeatedly said it is targeting armed groups that threaten Pakistan’s security, while Afghan and Western officials have historically pressed Pakistan to do more to prevent cross-border militant movement.

Across the border in Afghanistan, coalition forces and Afghan troops were involved in several clashes with Taliban fighters, military officials said. The fighting reportedly broke out after insurgents attacked patrols and outposts in eastern and southern provinces, areas where the Taliban has maintained a significant presence.

Coalition officials said air support was called in during at least one engagement after troops came under fire. Taliban spokesmen, in statements to media outlets, claimed responsibility for attacks on foreign and Afghan forces, though their casualty claims could not be independently verified.

The latest violence highlights the persistent instability in the border region, where militant groups exploit difficult terrain, porous crossings and limited government presence. Analysts say security operations on one side of the border often push fighters into the other, complicating efforts by both governments and international forces to contain the insurgency.

Pakistan’s military has carried out multiple campaigns in the northwest over the past two decades, including operations aimed at dismantling militant sanctuaries in areas such as North Waziristan, South Waziristan and Khyber. While officials say those offensives weakened insurgent networks, sporadic attacks and cross-border violence have continued.

Afghanistan has also seen repeated cycles of fighting between Taliban militants and Afghan or foreign-backed forces, particularly in rural districts where government control has often been contested.

Officials in Islamabad and Kabul have not announced any joint operation, but both sides have said they remain committed to securing the frontier. Diplomats have warned that without greater coordination, militants could continue to take advantage of gaps between the two countries’ security efforts.

The humanitarian impact of the fighting remains unclear. Aid groups have previously warned that military operations in Pakistan’s northwest and clashes in Afghanistan can displace thousands of civilians, many of whom have limited access to shelter, health care and food.

For now, residents on both sides of the border are bracing for more violence as security forces press their operations and Taliban fighters continue to mount attacks in contested areas.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a detailed news story about escalating Taliban violence in Pakistan and Afghanistan, mentioning South Waziristan/Khyber, Robert Gates' comments, Uruzgan fighting, NATO incidents, and the June coalition death toll.
counterfactuals.output:
**Taliban Violence Escalates Across Pakistan and Afghanistan as Coalition Losses Mount**

**ISLAMABAD/KABUL —** Taliban-linked militants intensified attacks on both sides of the Pakistan-Afghanistan border this week, deepening concerns that the insurgency is expanding its reach from Afghanistan’s southern battlefields into Pakistan’s tribal belt and beyond.

In Pakistan, security officials reported fresh militant activity in **South Waziristan** and the **Khyber** tribal region, two strategically important areas along the Afghan frontier. South Waziristan has long been a base for Pakistani Taliban factions and foreign militants, while Khyber is especially sensitive because it sits astride key routes used to move supplies toward NATO forces in Afghanistan.

Pakistani authorities said militants in the tribal areas had stepped up attacks on security posts, convoys and rival tribal groups, underscoring the government’s difficulty in containing insurgent networks that operate across rugged border terrain. The violence has fueled fears in Islamabad and Western capitals that militant sanctuaries in Pakistan are helping sustain the Taliban campaign inside Afghanistan.

Across the border, fighting also intensified in southern Afghanistan, particularly in **Uruzgan province**, where Afghan and international forces clashed with Taliban fighters in a series of engagements. NATO officials said coalition troops, alongside Afghan security forces, were battling insurgents attempting to expand their influence in rural districts and disrupt government control.

The fighting in Uruzgan comes amid a broader rise in Taliban attacks across Afghanistan’s south and east, including roadside bombings, ambushes and assaults on police outposts. Afghan officials say insurgents have increasingly relied on improvised explosive devices and suicide attacks, tactics that have contributed to rising casualties among Afghan civilians, government forces and foreign troops.

The deteriorating security picture was underscored by comments from U.S. Defense Secretary **Robert Gates**, who acknowledged the growing intensity of the Afghan conflict and warned that the Taliban remained a resilient enemy. Gates said the increase in violence reflected both the insurgency’s determination and the fact that more coalition forces had moved into contested areas, bringing them into more frequent contact with Taliban fighters.

His remarks came as NATO faced a series of difficult incidents in Afghanistan, including combat engagements and episodes that raised concern over civilian casualties and the risks of operating in heavily populated areas. NATO commanders have repeatedly said the Taliban deliberately fight from villages and use civilians as cover, while Afghan leaders have urged international forces to take greater care to avoid civilian deaths, which have become a major source of public anger.

The month of **June** has been especially costly for the U.S.-led coalition. Coalition fatalities in Afghanistan reached one of the highest monthly totals of the war, with more foreign troops killed there than in Iraq during the same period. The toll has reinforced the view among military analysts that Afghanistan, once treated as a secondary front after the 2003 invasion of Iraq, has again become a central battlefield for Western forces.

The surge in violence has placed additional pressure on both Kabul and Islamabad. Afghan officials have urged Pakistan to crack down harder on militant havens in the tribal areas, while Pakistan argues that it is fighting its own costly war against extremist groups and cannot rely on military force alone. Pakistan has alternated between military operations, local peace deals and political outreach, but critics say cease-fire arrangements have often given militants time to regroup.

For NATO, the escalating violence presents a strategic challenge. Commanders say more troops and better coordination with Afghan forces are needed to hold territory after clearing operations. But rising casualties, civilian harm and instability in Pakistan’s borderlands have complicated efforts to build public support for a long-term campaign.

Western officials increasingly describe the conflict as a regional war, with the insurgency drawing strength from networks that straddle the frontier. The latest fighting in South Waziristan, Khyber and Uruzgan suggests that the Taliban and allied militant groups remain capable of mounting pressure on multiple fronts at once — against Pakistan’s state authority, Afghanistan’s fragile government and the NATO-led coalition backing it.

counterfactuals.output:
ISLAMABAD, Pakistan (CNN) -- Pakistani forces pressed a major offensive against Taliban militants in the country’s northwest, the largest military push since the civilian government took power, officials said, as fighting sent thousands of civilians fleeing and raised new questions about the insurgency’s strength.

The operation, focused on militant positions in and around the Swat Valley and neighboring districts, followed the collapse of a controversial peace deal that had allowed the Taliban to impose a harsh version of Islamic law in parts of the region.

Pakistan’s military said troops used artillery, helicopter gunships and ground forces to target militant hideouts, command posts and supply routes. Military officials reported dozens of militants killed in recent clashes, though casualty figures could not be independently verified because journalists have limited access to the conflict zone.

A military spokesman said security forces were trying to avoid civilian casualties while “clearing the area of terrorists who challenged the writ of the state.”

“The operation will continue until the militants are eliminated or lay down their arms,” the spokesman said.

Local officials and aid groups said civilians were leaving the area in large numbers, many carrying only what they could gather before escaping the fighting. Families crowded into temporary camps or stayed with relatives in nearby towns.

“We left when the shelling got close,” one displaced resident said. “There was no food, no electricity, and we were afraid for our children.”

The offensive marks a significant test for Pakistan’s civilian leadership, which has faced pressure at home and abroad to confront Taliban fighters who expanded their influence from tribal areas along the Afghan border into settled districts closer to the capital, Islamabad.

Prime Minister Yousaf Raza Gilani defended the military action, saying the government had sought peace but militants had violated agreements and terrorized local communities.

“We tried dialogue, but they challenged the constitution and the authority of the state,” Gilani said. “The government will not allow Pakistan to be held hostage by extremists.”

The fighting comes as U.S. officials have grown increasingly alarmed by the Pakistani Taliban’s advance. A Pentagon assessment described the insurgency as resilient and increasingly capable, warning that militant groups in Pakistan’s border regions continue to threaten both Pakistan’s stability and U.S.-led efforts in neighboring Afghanistan.

Defense officials have said Taliban and al Qaeda-linked fighters use sanctuaries in Pakistan to plan attacks, recruit fighters and move weapons across the porous border. The Pentagon assessment said Pakistan’s willingness and ability to sustain pressure on militants would be critical to reversing insurgent gains.

U.S. officials publicly welcomed Pakistan’s operation but cautioned that military force alone would not be enough. They said Islamabad must also provide security, restore basic services and help displaced civilians return home.

Analysts said the offensive could become a turning point if the army holds territory after clearing militants, something it has struggled to do in past campaigns.

“The question is not whether the military can push the Taliban out temporarily,” one security analyst said. “The question is whether the government can come back in — with police, courts, schools and administration — so the militants don’t return.”

For civilians trapped in the conflict zone, the immediate concern remained survival.

“We don’t know when we can go back,” another displaced man said. “We only know that our homes are there, and the fighting is there too.”
